analysis.one_liner: Makes drug makers repay Medicare when their drug prices rise faster than inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and its health subcommittee but never received a markup or a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require manufacturers of Medicare Part B drugs—doctor-administered drugs without a cheaper generic competitor—to pay a rebate to Medicare whenever a drug's price rises faster than general inflation. The rebates would go back into the Medicare trust fund, and seniors' 20% coinsurance on those drugs would be recalculated off the inflation-adjusted price instead of the inflated one. The bill never moved after being referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees in April 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who use high-cost, doctor-administered drugs with no generic competition. If those drugs' prices climb faster than inflation, the government clawed back the excess and patients' coinsurance would be based on the inflation-adjusted price, not the inflated sticker price. Medicare's trust fund also gains the rebate money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on costly Part B drugs

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers of single-source Part B drugs (drugs or biologics with no direct generic or biosimilar competitor, costing $100 or more per patient per year) to pay Medicare a rebate each quarter equal to billing units times the amount their payment level exceeds an inflation-adjusted benchmark.

For covered drugs, patients' 20% Part B coinsurance would be computed from the inflation-adjusted payment amount rather than the actual inflated price, so cost-sharing stops growing with price gouging.
Rebate amounts would be deposited into the Federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund, offsetting Medicare spending.

Manufacturers that fail to pay would face a civil money penalty of at least 125% of the owed rebate, and the Secretary could study extending the rebate to multi-source drugs and Medicare Advantage plans.

The bill includes carve-outs to avoid disrupting supply: drugs on the FDA shortage list may have rebates reduced or waived, and drugs already discounted under the 340B program or Medicaid are excluded from rebate units.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers—especially makers of expensive biologics and other single-source Part B drugs—would pay rebates whenever their prices outpace inflation, and would face penalties of at least 125% of the owed amount for nonpayment. That cost pressure would reduce the revenue growth those companies could take from Medicare.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only single-source drugs paid under Part B; it excludes retail Part D drugs, many other billing arrangements, and multiple-source drugs, at least initially—only a study and possible later rulemaking would extend coverage, so much price gouging outside this narrow lane would continue.

The inflation benchmark is tied to 2015 price levels and to the Consumer Price Index, and new drugs get their own benchmark quarter after launch, so manufacturers keep full pricing freedom in a drug's launch window.

Rebates could discourage launch pricing or affect supply of some drugs; the bill responds by letting the Secretary waive rebates for drugs on the shortage list, but critics could argue this is a sign the policy could strain supply in marginal cases.
Rebates flow to the Medicare trust fund rather than directly to patients at the pharmacy; the patient benefit works only indirectly, through the recalculated coinsurance on covered drugs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, documented problem: Medicare Part B drug prices have historically risen faster than inflation, and patients share in that increase through coinsurance. Its scope is deliberately narrow—single-source drugs above a small cost floor, with shortage and 340B carve-outs—which lowers the risk of disrupting supply but also leaves most of the drug market untouched. On balance it is a targeted consumer-protection measure whose main cost falls on manufacturers of monopoly-priced drugs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and to the Health subcommittee in April 2021, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the bill on April 20, 2021, joined by three cosponsors, all Democrats.
The same day, the bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Committee on Ways and Means, and to the Health and Social Security subcommittees.
No further action—no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote—appears in the action history for the remainder of the 117th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of high-priced single-source Part B drugs are better off: they keep the freedom to raise prices above inflation with no rebate obligation, and Medicare beneficiaries continue to share those price increases through coinsurance.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows how the parties would have lined up.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug makers (especially makers of single-source Part B drugs and biologics)
industries.note: The bill forces quarterly rebates to Medicare whenever prices on monopoly-priced Part B drugs rise faster than inflation, with a penalty of at least 125% for nonpayment, directly capping the price growth these companies can charge seniors.

Biosimilars are included in the rebate definition, but the bill's pressure on brand-name price increases could strengthen the case for cheaper competitors; the net effect on this industry is unclear from the bill text.
